questions.question: What are primary minerals? Give one example.
questions.solution_html:
• What are primary minerals? Give one example.
  • Primary minerals are minerals that have not been altered chemically since their formation; they are
  • derived directly from the parent rock during the solidification of magma.
  • Examples: Quartz, Feldspar, Mica, Hornblende. Any other.

questions.question: What is soil science?
questions.solution_html:
• What is soil science?
  • Soil science is the study of soil as a natural resource, including its formation, classification, physical,
  • chemical, and biological properties, and its relationship to plant growth and the environment.

questions.question: Differentiate soil profile and soil horizon.
questions.solution_html:
• Differentiate soil profile and soil horizon.
  • Soil Profile: A soil profile is a vertical section of the soil from the surface down to the unaltered parent
  • material, showing all its distinct layers . It provides a snapshot of soil formation, composition, and
  • structure.
  • Soil horizon: A soil horizon is a distinct layer of soil within a soil profile that has different physical,
  • chemical, and biological characteristics from the layers above and below it. Each horizon forms due to
  • soil-forming processes like organic matter accumulation, leaching, and mineral weathering.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: soil-forming processes like organic matter accumulation, leaching, and mineral weathering.

questions.question: What is soil air, and how does its composition differ from atmospheric air?
questions.solution_html:
• What is soil air and how does its composition differ from atmospheric air?
  • Soil air is the gaseous phase present in the pore spaces of soil, which fills the spaces not occupied by
  • water or soil particles. It is essential for root respiration, microbial activity, and overall soil health. Soil
  • air has lower concentration of oxygen and higher concentration of CO2 compared to atmospheric air due
  • to root respiration and microbial activity.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: to root respiration and microbial activity.

questions.question: What does the term "time" refer to in soil formation, and why is it classified as a passive factor?
questions.solution_html:
• What does the term “time” refer to in soil formation and why is it classified as a passive factor?
  • In soil science, time refers to the duration over which soil -forming processes act on parent material to
  • develop distinct soil properties and horizons. It is essentially the age of the soil and the length of
  • exposure to factors like climate, organisms, and topography. Time considered as a passive factor
  • because time does not actively cause soil formation; instead, it allows other factors (climate, organisms,
  • relief, parent material) to work.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: relief, parent material) to work.

questions.question: What factors influence the particle density of a soil?
questions.solution_html:
• What factor influence the particle density of soil?
  • Particle density (ρₚ) refers to the mass of solid soil particles per unit volume, ty pically expressed in
  • g/cm³. It usually ranges from 2.60 to 2.75 g/cm³ for mineral soils. Particle density is influenced by the
  • type and composition of soil minerals rather than the pore space.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: type and composition of soil minerals rather than the pore space.

questions.question: Name and briefly describe four common soil structure types.
questions.solution_html:
• Name and briefly describe four common soil structure types.
  • Soil structure refers to the arrangement of soil particles into aggregates or peds, which affects water
  • movement, aeration, and root growth. Here are four common types:
  • • Granular Structure: Small, rounded aggregates resembling breadcrumbs.
  • • Blocky Structure: Soil forms irregular, roughly cube-shaped blocks.
  • • Platy Structure: Description: Soil arranged in thin, horizontal plates stacked like sheets.
  • • Prismatic/Pillar Structure: Vertical columns or pillars of soil, often capped on top.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: • Prismatic/Pillar Structure: Vertical columns or pillars of soil, often capped on top.

questions.question: What are the differences between Monomineralanic and polymineralanic rocks.
questions.solution_html:
• What are the differences between monomineralic and polymineralic rocks.
  • Page 3 of 4
  • A monomineralic rock is a rock that is composed predominantly or entirely of a single mineral. These
  • rocks have a uniform composition, color, and texture because only one mineral type dominates.
  • A polymineralic rock is a rock composed of two or more different minerals. These minerals occur
  • together in varying proportions, giving the rock a varied colour, texture, and composition.
questions.source_exam: Third Semester MGU-UGP(Hons.) Regular Exam Oct 2025
questions.final_answer: together in varying proportions, giving the rock a varied colour, texture, and composition.

questions.question: What is enriched compost? Discuss how compost can be enriched with essential nutrients like nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium, and bioinoculants.
questions.solution_html:
• What is enriched compost? discuss how compost can be enriched with essential nutrients like nitrogen,
  • phosphorus, potassium and bioinoculants?
  • Enriched compost is organic matter that has been decomposed and supplemented with additional
  • nutrients or beneficial microorganisms to enhance its fertility and effectiveness as a soil amendment.
  • Unlike ordinary compost, which primarily improves soil structure and moisture retention, enriched
  • Page 4 of 4
  • compost provides essential plant nutrients and supports microbial activity, making it a more effective
  • organic fertilizer.
  • Importance of Enriched Compost
  • • Supplies macro- and micronutrients to plants.
  • • Improves soil structure, aeration, and water-holding capacity.
  • • Enhances microbial activity, promoting nutrient cycling.
  • • Reduces dependence on chemical fertilizers, supporting sustainable agriculture.
  • Enrichment with Essential Nutrients
